[REDACTED]\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 937  ROLE: user\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\n<user_query>
will this speed the loop up and what is the loops max speed
</user_query>\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 938  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\n### Will this speed the loop up?

**Not in the sense of “raising the clock rate.”** The firmware **intentionally** runs one iteration about every **`STEP_US`** microseconds. At the end it sleeps so each pass takes **~`STEP_US`** (e.g. **250 µs → ~4000 loops/s**). That target is set by **`STEP_US`**, not by how much code you skip.

What **does** improve:

- **Less work per iteration** when WiFi is off and optional 1 Hz streams are off → less chance the CPU **overruns** the interval.
- If the body ever took **longer than `STEP_US`**, the sleep shrinks or vanishes (`remaining ≤ 0`), so timing gets **jittery**. Trimming work makes it easier to **actually hit** the intended **`STEP_US`** cadence.

So: it can make the loop **more stable** and closer to the designed rate; it does **not** magic increase **`1/STEP_US`** — that still comes from **`STEP_US`** in `pico_control_script.py`.

---

### What is the loop’s “max speed”?

**Target (design):**

\[
f_{\text{loop}} \approx \frac{1}{\texttt{STEP\_US}}
\]

with **`STEP_US` in seconds**. Examples:

| `STEP_US` | ~loops per second |
|-----------|-------------------|
| 250 µs    | **4000**          |
| 200 µs    | **5000**          |
| 400 µs    | **2500**          |

That is the **scheduled** main-loop rate.

**Practical cap:** each iteration must finish **serial poll + all `axis.update()` + optional POS/PINS + sleep** within that window. If work is too heavy, you **can’t** sustain a higher rate without **lowering `STEP_US`** in the file or **cutting work** further.

**Separate from loop rate:** per joint, the average **full-step rate** toward the host is limited by **`max_sps`** and burst **`MAX_STEPS_PER_AXIS_TICK`** in firmware (`_host_follow_budget`), not by the loop number alone.

**Bottom line:** “Loop max speed” ≈ **`1/STEP_US`** as a **target**; the WiFi/off-stream changes help you **actually meet** that target more reliably, not replace **`STEP_US`**.

[REDACTED]\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 939  ROLE: user\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\n<user_query>
what is the fastest the loop could run
</user_query>\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 940  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nThere isn’t a single fixed “max Hz” in the repo — the loop is **scheduled** by **`STEP_US`**, so the **target** rate is:

\[
f_{\text{target}} \approx \frac{1}{\texttt{STEP\_US}} \quad (\texttt{STEP\_US} \text{ in seconds})
\]

So in principle you could set **`STEP_US` very small** and ask for a **very high** target rate.

**What actually sets the fastest it can run** is **physics of one iteration**: everything in one pass must finish **before** the next `STEP_US` “slot,” or you lose timing (sleep goes to zero, steps bunch up, jitter).

Rough buckets:

| Factor | Why it limits top speed |
|--------|-------------------------|
| **`axis.update()`** | Each full step can cost real time (especially **NEMA** `sleep_us` edges per step; you can emit **several** steps per axis per tick). |
| **Number of axes** | Work adds **in series** in the `for axis in axes` loop. |
| **Serial poll + `_handle_line`** | Chars and full lines when the host is flooding. |
| **POS/PINS / homing / de‑energise** | Extra work when those features are active. |
| **MicroPython** | Interpreter overhead per loop — usually **much** lower ceiling than raw C on the same MCU. |

So:

- **Fastest the loop “could” run** ≈ **shortest `STEP_US` for which the real iteration time is still &lt; `STEP_US`”.**  
  There is **no constant** in firmware like “max 10 kHz”; you find the limit by **lowering `STEP_US`** until motion/serial misbehaves or you see instability.

**Ballpark intuition** (not a guarantee for *your* script): with **heavy** stepping + MicroPython, staying in the **low‑tens of kHz** target range is often optimistic; **a few kHz to ~10 kHz class** targets are more common unless you strip the loop down or move stepping to **timers/PWM/C** (Grbl-style).

**Bottom line:** The **ceiling** is **not** “`1/STEP_US` forever” — it’s **`1 / (time actually spent in one iteration)`**, and that time is dominated by **motor stepping** and **Python**, not WiFi (which you already disabled by default).

[REDACTED]\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 941  ROLE: user\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\n<user_query>
what is the fastest it could possibly go with the hardware we have
</user_query>\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 942  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\n“Fastest it could possibly go” splits into **what the electronics allow** vs **what your current Pico + MicroPython + this firmware loop can sustain**.

### 1. Electrical / motor hardware (upper bound in principle)

- **Step/dir drivers (A4988, DRV8825, many TMC boards)**  
  Datasheets often allow **very high** toggle rates on **STEP** (hundreds of kHz in principle), but you almost never run there on a mechanism: torque falls, resonance, and missed steps show up first. In practice people run **on the order of thousands to tens of thousands of full steps per second per motor** before the *mechanics* complain, not the chip’s absolute max pin frequency.

- **28BYJ + ULN2003**  
  These are **much slower** than NEMA+proper driver: real-world reliable rates are often **hundreds** of full steps per second **per motor**, not 10k+, especially under load.

- **Wiring / 3.3 V vs 5 V drivers**  
  Wrong level shifting can make **high speeds fail sooner**, but that’s reliability, not a sharp “MHz” limit from the Pico.

So the **hard ceiling** is **not** the RP2040 GPIO MHz number — it’s **driver + motor + load** (and cooling, resonance).

### 2. Your firmware path on the Pico (realistic ceiling)

- The **arm code doesn’t run “as fast as the CPU allows.”** It runs a **timed loop** (`STEP_US`) and does **MicroPython** + **GPIO** + sometimes **multiple steps per axis per tick**.

- **NEMA branch** uses short `sleep_us` around each STEP edge — that alone sets a **minimum time per full step** on that joint (on the order of **tens of µs per step**, not nanoseconds). So **per-axis** full-step rate from bit-banging is on the rough order of **tens of kHz** only if the rest of the loop were free — but the **whole** loop must also do **all other joints, serial, etc.**

- **MicroPython** adds overhead per iteration, so the **main loop** is usually **a few kHz to maybe low tens of kHz** *target* before things get ugly — and your **effective** command rate is further bounded by **`max_sps`**, **`MAX_STEPS_PER_AXIS_TICK`**, and **`STEP_US`**.

### 3. One concise statement

- **“Hardware alone” (drivers + motors, ignoring your code):** you could imagine **very high** step line toggle rates (often **100 kHz–class** in datasheets), but **meaningful motion** for a real arm is almost always **limited well below that** by **mechanics and tuning** — **kHz per motor** is already “fast” in mechanical terms.

- **“With what you actually have (Pico 2W + MicroPython + this firmware):”** the **practical** top end is **dominated by the control loop and bit-banged stepping**, not by the raw CPU MHz. You’ll find it by **lowering `STEP_US` and/or raising per-tick stepping** until torque drops or timing falls apart — there’s **no single number** in the repo that says “max 12.4 kHz forever”; it’s **the minimum period where one full loop iteration still fits**.

If you tell me **which motors are on which joints** (28BYJ vs NEMA on J2, and driver type), a tighter band is possible — **28BYJ-dominated arms** are usually **much** slower in achievable full-step rate than **NEMA + DM542/TMC** builds.

}\n\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 982  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nHere’s what was going wrong and what we changed.

### Cause
Each control tick called `axis.update(dt)` **in index order**. For host follow, each stepper used up its whole step budget (up to `MAX_STEPS_PER_AXIS_TICK`) **before** the next joint ran. So in one tick you effectively got “all of J0’s burst, then all of J1’s, …”, which **looks like one joint at a time** and makes the last joint still moving when the others have stopped.

### Fix (firmware)
In `pico_control_script.py`:

1. **`_HOST_INTERLEAVE_STEPS = True`**  
   Turn off with `False` if you ever want the old “exhaust one axis per tick” behavior.

2. **`_interleave_plan_host_steps(tdt)`**  
   Same home/limit logic as before, plus one call to **`_host_follow_budget`** per axis per tick (so the rate cap is unchanged).

3. **Main loop**  
   After planning, it **round-robins** `_emit_n_toward_target(1)` across joints until no axis has budget left or no one can step—so you get **at most one step per joint per pass**, shuffled across joints.

4. **`_finalize_interleave_host`**  
   Keeps velocity reporting consistent with the old `(e_before - e_after) / dt` behavior.

5. **`update()`**  
   If interleaving is on, after the homing state machine it **`return`s** so host follow is **only** driven from the main loop (homing still uses the full `update()` path).

6. **Finalize is skipped while `_homing_mode`** so we don’t reuse stale `_interleave_e0` during homing.

Redeploy this script to the Pico (Hardware tab deploy) so the device runs the new loop. After that, coordinated streams should advance **all joints together** each tick instead of one after another.

}\n\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 1002  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nHere’s what was implemented.

### Behavior
- **`HOST_FOLLOW_MAX_SPS = N`**: Let **M** = largest stepper **`max_sps`** in **JOINTS**. If **M > N**, every stepper’s effective rate is multiplied by **N/M** (same ratios, peak joint = **N**). If **M ≤ N**, nothing changes (no scaling up).
- Example: **J2 = 10000**, **J0 = 5000**, **N = 4000** → scale = 0.4 → **J2 → 4000**, **J0 → 2000**.
- **N = 0** (default): cap is **off**; each joint keeps its Motor tab **`max_sps`**.

### Where it lives
1. **Firmware** (`pico_control_script.py`): injectable block **`HOST_FOLLOW_MAX_SPS`**, and **`_apply_host_follow_sps_cap(axes)`** right after axes are built. **`MOTORINFO`** mentions the setting.
2. **Deploy** (`micropython_deployer.py`): **`_inject_host_follow_max_sps`**, wired in **`deploy`** / **`deploy_wifi`** (after **`STEP_US`**).
3. **Hardware tab**: **Host max sps** spin box (0 = “off”). Stored as **`firmware_host_follow_max_sps`** in saved UI state.
4. **Animation** (`animation.py`): **`motor_rad_limits_from_joint_cfgs(..., host_follow_max_sps)`** uses the same rule and scales **`max_sps`** and **`accel`** so sim timing stays aligned with hardware.

Redeploy firmware after changing **Host max sps** so the Pico gets the new constant.

}\n\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 1023  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nHere’s what was going on.

### Why 24000 sps on J2 doesn’t beat J1

`max_sps` is **motor full steps per second** at the driver. What you see at the **joint / output** is:

**output °/s ≈ `max_sps ÷ (steps_per_rev × gear_ratio) × 360`**

From your `motor_config.json`:

| Joint | max_sps | steps/output rev | **≈ °/s @ output** |
|-------|---------|------------------|---------------------|
| J1    | 12 000  | 1600×20 = 32 000 | **135** |
| J2    | 24 000  | 1600×70 = 112 000 | **~77** |

So J2 is capped at **about half** the angular rate of J1 at the arm, even though its `max_sps` is doubled. The extra gear (70× vs 20×) needs **3.5× more motor steps per output degree**, and 2× `max_sps` only partly offsets that.

The **sim and firmware** both convert `max_sps` to **output radians/s** using that same `steps_out` (see `animation.motor_rad_limits_from_joint_cfgs` and the Pico follower). So the model is consistent; it’s not ignoring J2’s 24 000.

### What we changed in the UI

1. **Motor tab → “Steps/output”** now includes **`max_sps → ≈ X°/s @ output shaft`** and updates when you change max steps/s, SPR, or gear.
2. **“Max speed”** tooltip explains that **output** speed depends on gear + steps/rev, not raw sps alone.

### If you want J2 physically faster than J1

You need a **higher** ratio of\(\frac{\text{max\_sps}}{\text{steps\_per\_rev} \times \text{gear}}\) for J2 than for J1 (e.g. raise J2 `max_sps` a lot more, reduce driver microstepping / effective steps per rev if mis-set, or change the gearbox), until the shown **°/s** for J2 exceeds J1’s.

Coordinated moves still use **one duration for all joints**, set by the **most constrained** joint for that motion—but the angular limits above are what matter for comparing J1 vs J2 capability.

}\n\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 1038  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\n### What was going wrong

The Pico loop **always added** `max_sps × STEP_US` to the host-follow integrator **once per loop**, but the **real** time between loops **was not** always `STEP_US`.

- When **several joints** had large following error, the **interleaved stepping** inner loop did **more work** per iteration → longer iteration → **fewer** loops per second.
- When **J1/J2 (say) were almost on target**, that inner work **dropped** → iterations became **shorter**, sleep filled the rest of `STEP_US`, and you got **more** loops per second.
- **J0** still had a large error, so each extra loop still granted another **full** `STEP_US` slice of rate limit. Result: **J0’s motor got more “sps budget” per real second** when the other axes lightened their load — often **mid-move**, which matches “halfway through it speeds up.”

So this was a **timing / budgeting mismatch** (fixed `dt` vs real inter-loop time), not the sim smoothstep or J0 alone.

### What we changed

In `pico_control_script.py` the main loop now:

1. Measures **actual** microseconds since the **previous** loop start (`du_us`), with a sensible cap for long stalls.
2. Uses **`tdt = du_us × 1e⁻⁶`** for **`update()` / `_interleave_plan_host_steps` / `_finalize_interleave_host`** so host-follow rate tracks **wall-clock** time.
3. Replaces the old **`tick_us += STEP_US`** sleep with **sleep from this loop’s start** so the period still targets **`STEP_US`**, without the catch-up behavior that pumped extra iterations.

Redeploy firmware to the Pico so this runs on hardware.

If anything still feels off after deploy, say whether you see it **only with hardware** or also in the **3D sim** (the fix is firmware-only).

### Cause
1. **Pico** — Host follow turned **full `max_sps` on immediately** each tick (only limited by error and burst cap). There was **no** ramp, so motion felt sharp at start/stop and when targets updated.
2. **Simulator** — `smoothstep` used a **`t^0.8` warp** before the quintic, which skews motion toward an aggressive “ease-in” and is **not** symmetric, so acceleration isn’t as smooth as a classic ease.

### Changes

**1. Firmware (`pico_control_script.py`)**  
- Host follow now uses a **signed velocity** state with:
  - **`accel`** from the Motor tab (steps/s²). If deploy has `accel: 0`, it defaults to about **`10 × max_sps`** so you still get a ramp without editing JSON.
  - A **braking cap**: cruise speed is limited by `min(max_sps, sqrt(2 * accel * remaining_distance))` so the axis can slow in time before the next target.
- **`STOP` / `SYNC`** call `clear_host_follow_rates()` so integrators don’t carry across resets.
- **`HOST_FOLLOW_MAX_SPS`** scaling now scales **`accel`** by the same factor as **`max_sps`** so ramps stay consistent when the global cap is on.
- **`MOTORINFO`** text mentions accel-based ramping.

**2. Simulator (`animation.py`)**  
- **`smoothstep`** is the **plain quintic** smootherstep on `[0,1]` (same end conditions, **symmetric** ease, smoother acceleration profile in the GUI).

**3. GUI**  
- **Accel** tooltip notes that Deploy sends it to the Pico for **host-follow ramping**.

Redeploy firmware so the Pico runs the new follower. Tune **Accel** per joint on the Motor tab (lower = softer ramps; higher = quicker). **Jerk** in the UI is still sim-side only for now; the Pico uses the trapezoid-style **accel** limit.

}\n\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 1060  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\n### What was still causing the base surge

We started using **real time between loop starts** (`du_us`) as `tdt` for host-follow. That fixed “too many cheap iterations → burst.” It had a side effect:

- When **one loop is slow** (lots of interleaved steps on J1/J2), the **next** loop sees a **large** `du_us` (often **several × STEP_US**).
- That full interval was applied **once** to:
  - accel-limited **velocity**
  - `_host_follow_frac += |v| * tdt`
- So the **tick after a heavy iteration** could **inject a big chunk** of motion in one go. The base (J0) often still has a large following error, so it shows up there most.

### Fix

In `pico_control_script.py` we **cap** the `tdt` passed into all motor math at **`MOTION_DT_MAX_MULT × STEP_US`** (default **3×** the nominal control period).  

So even if the previous loop took 800 µs, the next motion update only integrates **at most ~3×** a single STEP_US slice, not the full 800 µs in one shot.

Redeploy firmware to the Pico so this runs on hardware.

If anything still feels sharp after that, the next place to tune is **host angle cadence** (serial stream) or slightly lowering **Accel** for the base on the Motor tab.

}\n\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 1064  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nHere’s how to make motion **faster** while keeping the **same kind** of smooth accel you have now.

### 1. Simulator (3D moves, IK, waypoints)
- **Animation → Speed** slider — `1.0x` is default; drag up to **5.0x** for shorter move time. Same path, less wall-clock time.
- **Motor configuration → Max speed (sps)** — raises the **limit** the sim uses when it computes move duration (with your gear, output °/s still depends on steps/rev × gear).
- **Motor configuration → Accel** — higher = **shorter ramp** (gets to cruise quicker). Too high can look rough on the real arm; tune by feel.

### 2. Physical arm (Pico)
Anything below needs **Deploy** so `JOINTS` and `STEP_US` match what you set.

- **Same Motor tab numbers**: **`max_sps`** = top cruise rate the Pico will allow toward the streamed target; **`accel`** = how fast it **ramps** to that rate (higher = snappier but still smooth).
- **Hardware → Host max sps** — if it’s not **off (0)** , it scales everyone down. Set **0** or raise the cap so the elbow isn’t throttled vs the base.
- **Hardware → STEP_US** — **smaller µs** ⇒ higher loop rate (e.g. 250 → 200). Only go as low as the Pico stays stable (no stalls / missed steps); if the loop overruns `STEP_US`, bump it back up.
- **USB baud** — e.g. **921600** if your stack supports it, so the **angle stream** can run at a higher Hz (the app caps stream rate from baud so the serial line doesn’t flood). Faster updates = the arm tracks a moving target more closely and can feel “faster” in practice.

### 3. Quick mental model
- **Faster overall motion** → raise **`max_sps`** (within motor/driver limits).  
- **Faster ramp (still smooth)** → raise **`accel`**, not `max_sps` alone.  
- **Sim finishes before the real arm** → increase deployed **`max_sps` / `accel`**, improve **stream rate** (baud / STEP_US), or relax **Host max sps**.

If you tell me whether “slow” is mostly in the **3D sim**, the **real arm**, or **both**, we can narrow to one knob set—but the list above is the full toolbox you already have.

</user_query>\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 1066  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nFor **only the 3D arm** (viewport + timed moves), speed mainly comes from these **in the app**—no Pico deploy:

### 1. **Animation → Speed**
Use the **Speed** slider (default **1.0×**, up to **5.0×**). That scales how long each move takes: **higher = faster** for the same path.

### 2. **Motor configuration**
Values here drive **how fast the simulator is allowed to say the arm can move** (then the animator picks duration):

- **Max speed (sps)** — higher → higher effective joint speed limits → **shorter** moves (especially on heavy‑gear joints).
- **Accel (sps²)** — higher → the “allowed” acceleration in the motor model is larger → moves can **finish sooner** while still respecting the trapezoid/smoothstep math.

Use **Motor configuration → Save** so `motor_config.json` keeps them.

### 3. **If something still feels capped**
Moves are limited by the **slowest joint** on that path (status bar can mention which joint sets duration). Raising **max sps** / **accel** on that bottleneck joint—or fixing an **overstated gear ratio**—speeds the **whole** coordinated move.

**TL;DR:** turn **Animation → Speed** up first; then raise **Motor max sps** (and **accel** if ramps feel slow) for joints that still limit the motion.

### Why the real arm fell behind the 3D animation
- The **on-screen arm** is updated every **timer tick** (~1 kHz) while a move is running.
- **USB** only sends `J0:…,J1:…` lines at a **capped rate** derived from baud (often **~100–150 lines/s** at 115200), and the GUI also used a **conservative** cap when **not** animating.
- **WiFi** didn’t expose a baud for that math, so the GUI always assumed **`baud is None`** and fell back to **`5 ms`** between lines (**200 Hz**), which is coarse for a smooth轨迹.

So the **Pico was chasing a staircase of targets** much sparser than the 3D path — it **couldn’t** stay in time with the viewport.

### What we changed
1. **`gui.py` — `_hardware_angle_stream_min_interval_s`**  
   While **`animator.is_running`**, the target stream rate is pushed up toward the **link‑limited** value (roughly **`0.92 × max_line_hz`**, with a **100–330 Hz** band) instead of the old **35–200 Hz** idle cap. That sends **many more** pose updates during a scripted move so hardware can track the animation.

2. **`pico_wifi_interface.py`**  
   Set a nominal **`self._baud = 921600`** (TCP isn’t UART; it’s only used for the **same** line‑rate estimate as USB) so WiFi no longer always uses the **200 Hz** fallback.

Reconnect once and run a move: you should see the physical arm **follow the 3D motion more closely** during animation.

**Still won’t be sample‑perfect**: the Pico also **ramps** motion in firmware, so a tiny phase lag can remain. For the tightest match, use **higher USB baud** (e.g. **460800** / **921600** if your cable/driver allows) and keep **“Enable hardware sync”** on. If anything still drifts, say whether you’re on **USB** or **WiFi**.

</user_query>\n\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nENTRY 1086  ROLE: assistant\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------\nYou can make things “faster” in **three separate places**: the **3D sim**, the **commanded motion** (Motor tab / animation), and the **real arm** (firmware + link). They don’t all do the same job.

### 1. Faster motion in the **3D view** (simulator only)

- **Animation → Speed** (slider, default `1.0×`, up to `5.0×`): shortens **wall-clock time** for the same path. The viewport and `arm_state` run faster; this is independent of the Pico.

- **Motor configuration → Max speed (sps)** and **Accel**: used when the **Animator** picks **move duration** from motor limits (`motor_rad_limits_from_joint_cfgs` in `animation.py`). Higher **max_sps** → higher allowed angular rate (after converting steps/s to rad/s using steps/rev × gear). Higher **accel** → the trapezoid/smoothstep duration math allows **shorter** moves for the same angle change.

- **Important**: “Output” speed at the joint is **not** raw `max_sps`; it’s proportional to `max_sps ÷ (steps_per_rev × gear_ratio)` in °/s at the shaft. So raising **gear** in the model without raising **max_sps** can make the arm **slower** in the sim.

**Tradeoff:** Very high animation speed or limits can make moves so short they feel snappy or hard to follow on screen; that’s a UX choice, not hardware.

---

### 2. Faster **physical arm** (must match after **Deploy**)

What actually limits the real joints is **on the Pico** in **`JOINTS`** after deploy:

- **`max_sps`**: upper bound on **motor full steps per second** when following streamed angles.

- **`accel`**: how aggressively the firmware can **ramp** toward that speed (you added smooth accel-limited following in firmware).

- **Hardware → Host max sps**: if not **off (0)**, it **scales all steppers** so the fastest joint’s effective rate is capped — raising this cap (or turning it off) allows higher speeds.

- **Hardware → STEP_US**: smaller µs ⇒ **higher intended control-loop rate**; only helps if the loop keeps up. If you go too low, the Pico may overrun its period and motion gets worse, not faster.

**Tradeoff:** Higher **max_sps** / lower **STEP_US** can cause **missed steps**, driver faults, or USB overload depending on mechanics and wiring. Tune up gradually.

---

### 3. **Sim and hardware “in sync”** (feeling fast *and* together)

The PC sends **`J0:…,J1:…`** lines at a **limited rate** (from serial baud and GUI throttling). The **3D arm** updates much more often than that. So:

- **Higher USB baud** (e.g. 460800, 921600 if stable) allows **more angle lines per second** → the real arm tracks the interpolated path more closely and can **keep up** with faster sim motion.

- **WiFi** path uses a nominal baud hint for the same rate estimate; LAN is usually not the bottleneck, but the **GUI still rate-limits** sends.

**Tradeoff:** Flooding the serial port can drop lines and make motion **worse**; the app deliberately caps stream rate to avoid that.

---

### Practical order to try

| Goal | What to turn |
|------|----------------|
| Faster **on-screen** moves | Animation Speed, then Motor **max_sps** / **accel** |
| Faster **real** motion | Motor **max_sps** / **accel**, Deploy; adjust **Host max sps** / **STEP_US** |
| Sim and arm **track** better | Higher **baud**, keep hardware sync on, don’t run animation far faster than the stream can support |

If you say whether you mean **only the 3D model**, **only the physical arm**, or **both matched**, the shortest set of knobs narrows further.

  "contents": "# Robot Arm Simulator — Fab Academy Project Documentation\n\n**Document purpose:** Single-project documentation for Fab Academy portfolio / documentation repository.  \n**Project:** Desktop 3D robotic arm simulator with analytical inverse kinematics, constraints, animation, waypoint sequencing, and optional Raspberry Pi Pico 2W hardware synchronization.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Executive summary\n\nThis project is a **cross-platform desktop application** (Python, PyQt6, OpenGL) that models a **base-rotating planar manipulator** (SCARA-like convention): one revolute base joint plus *N* coplanar joints (typically 1–10 configurable links). It provides:\n\n- **Forward and inverse kinematics** with analytical 2R reduction and numerical fallback  \n- **Interactive 3D visualization**, IK-driven motion to workspace targets, and smooth time-based animation  \n- **Collision checks**, joint limits, singularity warnings, and optional **end-effector orientation** locking  \n- **Waypoint sequencing**, JSON import/export, terminal scripting (95+ commands), and optional **hardware bridge** to a **MicroPython** controller on a **Raspberry Pi Pico 2W**\n\nThe physical arm is treated as a **position follower**: the PC streams joint angles over USB serial or WiFi TCP; trajectory shaping (smooth paths, coordinated timing) is primarily computed on the host, while the firmware enforces **safe stepping**, optional **acceleration limiting**, and **gear-accurate** step counting.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Motivation & context (Fab Academy)\n\nFab Academy emphasizes **digital fabrication workflows**: design in software, iterate in simulation, then realize with machines. This tool supports that arc for **articulated mechanisms**:\n\n- Validate **reachability**, **singularities**, and **motion plans** before committing material  \n- Teach **kinematic conventions** (DH-style planar chains, base yaw, elbow modes) in an interactive setting  \n- Bridge to **embedded control** using an inexpensive **RP2040** board (Pico 2W) with **deploy-injected** motor parameters\n\nThe simulator is suitable as a **final project deliverable** artifact: runnable source, documented architecture, reproducible dependencies, and an optional hardware stack that maps cleanly to documentation (schematics, BOM, firmware blocks).\n\n---\n\n## 3. Repository layout\n\n```\nRobot Arm Sim/\n├── README.md                 # Quick install & feature list\n├── requirements.txt          # Python dependencies (repo root)\n├── FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md   # This file\n└── Robot-Arm-Sim/\n    ├── main.py               # Entry point: logging, dependency check, QApplication\n    ├── gui.py                # Main window: viewport, panels, timer (~1 kHz sim loop)\n    ├── kinematics.py         # FK, IK (analytical + numerical), Jacobian\n    ├── animation.py          # Smoothstep interpolation, motor-limited durations\n    ├── constraints.py        # Limits, collisions, orientation, singularity\n    ├── math_engine.py        # Sandboxed SymPy expressions for custom rules\n    ├── firmware/\n    │   └── pico_control_script.py   # MicroPython firmware template (deployed as main.py)\n    ├── hardware/\n    │   ├── protocol.py       # Angle line encoding, SYNC, thresholds\n    │   ├── pico_interface.py # USB serial (pyserial), TX queue\n    │   ├── pico_wifi_interface.py   # TCP client (same API as USB)\n    │   └── micropython_deployer.py   # Injects JOINTS, STEP_US, WiFi, caps into firmware\n    ├── config/               # arm_config.json, motor_config.json (GUI-driven)\n    ├── waypoints/            # Optional JSON sequences (auto-load supported)\n    ├── sim_terminal/         # Terminal command helpers & help text\n    └── tests/                # Acceptance & integration tests\n```\n\n---\n\n## 4. Technology stack\n\n| Layer | Technology |\n|-------|------------|\n| UI | PyQt6 |\n| 3D | pyqtgraph + PyOpenGL |\n| Numerics | NumPy |\n| Symbolic constraints | SymPy (sandboxed evaluation in `math_engine.py`) |\n| Embedded | MicroPython on Raspberry Pi Pico 2W |\n| PC ↔ MCU | USB CDC serial **or** WiFi TCP (same logical protocol) |\n\n**Runtime:** Python 3.11+ recommended (PyQt6 compatibility per project constraints).\n\n---\n\n## 5. Software architecture\n\n### 5.1 Main loop (`main.py`)\n\n- Configures logging (console + rotating `logs/hardware_log.txt` beside the executable or script root).  \n- Verifies dependencies unless frozen/packaged.  \n- Launches `QApplication` and `MainWindow` from `gui.py`.\n\n### 5.2 Simulation loop (`gui.py`)\n\nA **high-frequency timer** (default **1 ms → ~1000 Hz**) advances:\n\n1. **Animation** — `Animator.step(dt)` with wall-clock `dt` (capped after stalls).  \n2. **Rendering** — viewport updates are **decimated** (not every tick) to limit GPU load.  \n3. **Hardware** — when enabled, joint angles are sent to the Pico at a **rate derived from baud** (and higher during scripted animation so the physical arm tracks the on-screen trajectory more closely).\n\n### 5.3 Core modules\n\n| Module | Responsibility |\n|--------|------------------|\n| `kinematics.py` | Planar FK accumulation rotated by base angle; DH frames for Jacobian; analytical IK (2R core + tail distribution); numerical IK fallback |\n| `animation.py` | Quintic **smootherstep** path on `[0,1]` with zero velocity/acceleration at endpoints; motor-aware minimum duration using per-joint ω and α from motor configuration |\n| `constraints.py` | Joint limits, self-collision, table plane, singularity hints |\n| `math_engine.py` | User-supplied SymPy expressions per joint (advanced workflows) |\n\n### 5.4 Coordinate system\n\n- **+Z** is **up**; the **table** is the XY plane at **z = 0**.  \n- **Planar angle 0** means the corresponding link points along **+Z** (vertical).  \n- **Base angle** rotates the vertical plane about **Z** into **X/Y**.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Inverse kinematics (conceptual)\n\n1. **Base:** `atan2(y, x)` from target XY.  \n2. **Projection:** target projected into the vertical plane giving radial distance `r` and height `z`.  \n3. **Wrist reduction (N ≥ 3):** tail links aligned along an approach direction so a **2R** solve applies to the first two links toward a constructed wrist point.  \n4. **2R closed form:** law of cosines for elbow bend; **elbow up/down** selects root branch.  \n5. **Limits & fallback:** validate limits; optional numerical Jacobian iteration if analytical fails.\n\nOrientation locking adjusts the last planar joint during animation so the cumulative planar angle tracks a smoothed orientation target.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Simulation features (GUI)\n\n- **Configurable arm:** 1–10 planar joints, link lengths, plane offsets, base vertical offset.  \n- **IK:** analytical primary path; numerical fallback; elbow preference; EE orientation constraint (optional).  \n- **Animation:** motor-model-aware durations; global speed multiplier (**0.1×–5×**) on the Animation panel.  \n- **Waypoints:** ordered sequences, loop mode, JSON **v2.0** export/import including embedded arm configuration.  \n- **Terminal:** large command set for motion, poses, waypoints, viewport, macros, and hardware passthrough.  \n- **Hardware panel:** USB vs WiFi, connect/deploy, STEP_US and optional global step-rate cap, persistence in config JSON.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Hardware integration (Raspberry Pi Pico 2W)\n\n### 8.1 Conceptual split\n\n| Location | Role |\n|----------|------|\n| **PC** | IK, smooth paths, synchronized animation timing, angle streaming |\n| **Pico** | Parse `Jn:angle_deg` lines, map angles → motor steps, **accel-limited** velocity toward targets, optional homing state machines, optional WiFi TCP server |\n\nFirmware text emphasizes: **smoothing and coordination live on the host**; the device is a **faithful follower** with safety caps.\n\n### 8.2 Protocol (host → Pico)\n\nTypical line:\n\n```text\nJ0:12.34,J1:-5.67,J2:10.00,J3:0.00\\n\n```\n\nAngles are **degrees** in simulator convention; firmware converts using deployed **steps/rev**, **gear_ratio**, and **zero offsets**.\n\nSpecial forms include **`SYNC:`** (seed logical pose without a sprint after reconnect) and commands such as **`STOP`**, **`HOME`**, **`POS_STREAM_ON`**, documented in `hardware/protocol.py` and firmware comments.\n\n### 8.3 Deploy pipeline (`micropython_deployer.py`)\n\nDeploy reads `firmware/pico_control_script.py`, injects:\n\n- **`JOINTS`** block from Motor Configuration (GPIO, driver type, limits, homing pins, **max_sps**, **accel**, etc.)  \n- **`STEP_US`** (main-loop period, µs) from Hardware panel  \n- **`HOST_FOLLOW_MAX_SPS`** (optional global proportional cap on peak joint rate)  \n- **WiFi credentials** when SSID is non-empty (`ENABLE_WIFI`)\n\nUpload uses **raw USB REPL** (no strict dependency on `mpremote`) or **WiFi UPLOAD** protocol when redeploying over TCP.\n\n### 8.4 Supported motor personalities (firmware)\n\n- **28BYJ-48** + ULN2003 (4-wire half-step sequence)  \n- **Step/direction** (e.g. NEMA + A4988/DRV8825/TMC)  \n- **RC servo** (PWM) — position-only, no stepped follower dynamics  \n\nMixed configurations per joint index are supported.\n\n### 8.5 Practical tuning\n\n- **`max_sps`:** motor full-steps per second ceiling toward streamed targets (after gear, output shaft °/s is **`max_sps / (steps_per_rev × gear) × 360`**).  \n- **`accel`:** steps/s² — ramp rate on device toward cruise speed (smooth starts/stops).  \n- **`STEP_US`:** target loop period; shorten **only** if CPU reliably completes each iteration.  \n- **Serial baud:** higher baud allows **denser angle streams**, improving tracking versus the ~1 kHz sim (still intentionally capped to avoid USB saturation).\n\n---\n\n## 9. Configuration files\n\n| File | Role |\n|------|------|\n| `Robot-Arm-Sim/config/arm_config.json` | Link lengths, offsets, starting angles, UI persistence |\n| `Robot-Arm-Sim/config/motor_config.json` | Per-joint motor parameters consumed by Motor Configuration panel and deploy |\n\nPaths resolve relative to the runtime base directory (`main.py` / frozen exe).\n\n---\n\n## 10. Installation & running\n\n### From source\n\n```bash\ncd Robot-Arm-Sim\npip install -r ../requirements.txt\npython main.py\n```\n\n*(Some README variants reference `text files/requirements.txt`; use the repo root `requirements.txt` unless your checkout differs.)*\n\n### Dependencies (required)\n\n- PyQt6, pyqtgraph, PyOpenGL (+ accelerate), NumPy, SymPy  \n\n### Optional\n\n- **pyserial** — USB Pico connection  \n\n### Frozen executable\n\nThe repository README references `build_exe.bat` and `BUILD.md` for a standalone Windows `.exe` workflow.\n\n---\n\n## 11. Testing\n\nFrom project conventions:\n\n```bash\ncd Robot-Arm-Sim\npython -c \"import sys; sys.path.insert(0, '.'); exec(open('tests/test_acceptance.py').read())\"\npython -c \"import sys; sys.path.insert(0, '.'); exec(open('tests/test_integration.py').read())\"\n```\n\nExpect acceptance/integration suites to pass on a healthy checkout.\n\n---\n\n## 12. Design tradeoffs (honest summary)\n\n| Choice | Benefit | Cost |\n|--------|---------|------|\n| Analytical IK first | Fast, deterministic, explainable in docs | Must maintain geometric cases for N joints |\n| Host-side smoothing | Rich profiles without MCU FP overhead | Serial bandwidth caps tracking vs 3D |\n| Full-step firmware | Predictable on drivers listed | Sub-step micro interpolation not modeled |\n| Unified Pico script | One artifact to deploy | Large single file (MicroPython norm) |\n\n---\n\n## 13. ## Two different meanings of “firmware”

### 1. **Board firmware (UF2 — “flash the chip”)**

This repo **does not** provide two different UF2 images (e.g. “Wi‑Fi build” vs “non‑Wi‑Fi build”). You still use **one** MicroPython build meant for **Pico W** (from Raspberry Pi / MicroPython downloads). That build already includes what’s needed for Wi‑Fi on the **CYW43439**; there isn’t a second UF2 in this project that’s “only for Wi‑Fi.”

So: **no second UF2 to flash from this simulator** for Wi‑Fi specifically.

### 2. **Application “firmware” (`main.py` on the Pico)**

Everything for USB vs Wi‑Fi is **one Python script**: `Robot-Arm-Sim/firmware/pico_control_script.py`, deployed as **`main.py`**.

Wi‑Fi is **not** a separate file you flash—it’s **branches inside that script**, controlled by the injected block:

```49:56:Robot-Arm-Sim/firmware/pico_control_script.py
# WiFi is OFF unless you deploy with an SSID (sets ENABLE_WIFI True) or edit here.

# <<BEGIN_WIFI_CONFIG>>
ENABLE_WIFI = False
WIFI_SSID = ""
WIFI_PASSWORD = ""
TCP_PORT = 8888
# <<END_WIFI_CONFIG>>
```

On deploy, `micropython_deployer.py` sets **`ENABLE_WIFI = True`** only when you enter a **non‑empty SSID**; otherwise it stays **`False`** (“USB-only” behavior, with the deployer explicitly noting Wi‑Fi disabled for a faster control loop).

So the “separate Wi‑Fi behavior” you asked about is implemented as:

- **USB-only app**: deploy **without** SSID → `ENABLE_WIFI=False`, serial only.  
- **Wi‑Fi app**: deploy **with** SSID/password/port → `ENABLE_WIFI=True`, TCP server thread runs.

Same script, different injected constants—not two different UF2s.

### 3. **Updating over Wi‑Fi after it works**

Once the Pico is already running a build with **`ENABLE_WIFI=True`** and connected, the deployer can push a **new** `main.py` **over TCP** (`_deploy_via_wifi` with `UPLOAD_BEGIN` / chunks / `UPLOAD_END`). That still isn’t “a separate Wi‑Fi firmware binary”—it’s **replacing `main.py`** over the network.

---

## Practical answer

| Goal | What you do |
|------|----------------|
| “USB-only” runtime | Deploy with **blank SSID** (or edit template / manual deploy with `ENABLE_WIFI=False`). |
| “Wi‑Fi-enabled” runtime | Deploy with **SSID** (and password) so **`ENABLE_WIFI=True`** is injected. |
| Flash the chip once | Use **one** MicroPython **Pico W** UF2 from upstream; this project doesn’t maintain an alternate UF2 for Wi‑Fi. |

If you had in mind something else—**two physical UF2s**, or **forking** `pico_control_script.py` into separate USB vs Wi‑Fi-only files—say which you want and we can align the wording with your Fab docs.

## What exists today

When **`ENABLE_WIFI`** is true, the Pico starts a **TCP server on `TCP_PORT`** (default **8888**) and speaks the **same line-oriented protocol** as USB (`J0:…,J1:…`, etc.). There is **no HTTP stack** and **no browser UI** in that script yet—only raw sockets for commands and optional Wi‑Fi deploy (**`UPLOAD_*`**).

Limit/home wiring is already modeled per joint: optional **`home_pin`**, polarity, and **`at_home`** updated when the switch reads active (see the motor class around the homing/limit logic in ```238:408:Robot-Arm-Sim/firmware/pico_control_script.py```).

Joint targets are tracked as **steps → angles** using **`JOINTS`** (steps/rev, gear, offsets—the same block the GUI injects on deploy).

## What you’re asking for (web dashboard)

Conceptually it’s three layers:

| Piece | Role |
|--------|------|
| **HTTP server** on the Pico | Serves **HTML/CSS/JS** (and maybe `/api/state` JSON). |
| **Small REST or SSE/WebSocket API** | Returns joint angles, switch states, optional EE pose; accepts jog commands. |
| **Page JS** | Draws a simple 2D arm, polls or streams state, wires buttons. |

That **does not** require a second UF2: it’s still **`main.py`** MicroPython, extended with something like **MicroDot**, **Picoweb**, or a **minimal HTTP parser on `socket`** (you’d run it on **another port** (e.g. **8080**) or multiplex carefully so you don’t break the existing **8888** TCP protocol—or you dedicate one port to “machine protocol” and one to “human web UI,” which is usually clearer).

## Data the Pico can supply without the PC

- **Joint angles** — yes, from internal step counts and `JOINTS` geometry constants.
- **Limit/home dots** — yes, by exposing **`home_pin`** state / **`at_home`** (and any extra limit GPIOs you add later). Colors = pressed vs released in JSON → CSS in the page.
- **Buttons for per-joint jog** — yes: handlers translate “nudge J2 +0.5°” into updating internal targets (same idea as streaming angles, but **local deltas**), still respecting **`max_sps`**, **`accel`**, and software **`limit_min_deg` / `limit_max_deg`** if set.

## End-effector position and “jog EE along X”

- **Showing EE X/Y/Z (or X/Y in the vertical plane + base rotation)** needs **forward kinematics**. The simulator does full FK in Python on the PC; the Pico firmware **does not** currently ship that math. You **can** add a compact FK for **your** deployed geometry if you **inject link lengths** (same numbers as `arm_config`) into the firmware next to **`JOINTS`**—it’s duplicate logic and must stay in sync when you change the arm model.
- **Jogging the EE along the world X axis** is **Cartesian motion**, which requires **inverse kinematics** (or iterative Jacobian steps). Options:
  - **Implement a small IK** on the Pico for your specific arm (same duplication/sync risk as FK).
  - **Approximation**: tiny FK+nudge loop (“step X, solve approximate Δ joints”) — brittle and easy to get wrong.
  - **Split architecture**: Pico serves the UI but **browser talks to the PC** for IK — then it’s not a standalone Pico-only dashboard.

So: **visualizer + limits + joint readouts + joint jog** = very reasonable on-device. **EE position display** = reasonable if you accept **deploy-injected link lengths + ported FK**. **EE jog along X** = the hard part unless you port IK or relax to “jog in joint space only” on the web UI.

## Practical tradeoffs

- **RAM/CPU**: One HTTP worker + JSON + static assets fits Pico W if pages stay small; heavy Canvas 3D libraries are a bad fit—prefer **SVG or simple 2D canvas**.
- **Security**: Any Wi‑Fi HTTP interface on your LAN should be treated as **debug/control plane**—no auth in a minimal student project is common; document that it’s **not** internet-facing.
- **Two TCP services**: Keep **8888** for the simulator/reliability tooling if you want, add **8080** for HTTP, or merge protocols only if you’re disciplined about routing **HTTP** vs **text lines**.

## Summary

**Yes**, you can make the **Wi‑Fi build** open a **small web server** with a **dot-based limit visualization**, **live joints**, **EE coordinates**, and **joint jog buttons**, if you add HTTP + FK (and optionally IK for Cartesian EE jog). Nothing in the repo implements that yet; it’s an extension of **`pico_control_script.py`** plus embedded **HTML/JS** assets—not a separate UF2.

If you want this implemented in the repo next, say so explicitly (Agent mode); the explain-only mode stops at architecture like above.

## 1. `hardware/micropython_deployer.py`
- **`_generate_web_arm_block` / `_inject_web_arm_config`** — replaces the `# <<BEGIN_WEB_ARM_CONFIG>>` … `# <<END_WEB_ARM_CONFIG>>` section with:
  - `WEB_HTTP_PORT = 8080`
  - `ARM_LINK_LENGTHS`, `ARM_JOINT_PLANE_OFFSETS`, lateral offsets, `ARM_BASE_VERTICAL_OFFSET`
  - `ARM_JOINT_LIMITS_RAD` (from GUI joint limits, radians)
  - `IK_USE_ELBOW_DOWN` (from Arm panel: **Elbow Down** = index 0 → `True`)
- **`deploy()`** and **`deploy_wifi()`** take optional **`arm_config`** and call **`_inject_web_arm_config`** after WiFi injection.

## 2. `gui.py`
- USB and WiFi deploy both pass **`arm_config=self._get_arm_config_dict()`** so the Pico gets the same geometry as the simulator.

## 3. `firmware/pico_control_script.py`
- **`WEB_ARM_CONFIG`** block (defaults when not deployed / empty geometry).
- **FK** aligned with `kinematics.forward_kinematics` (including lateral offsets).
- **IK** for Cartesian **EE ±X** when lateral offsets are **zero** (same restriction as analytical IK on PC). If offsets are non‑zero, EE jog is skipped; joint jog still works.
- **`_web_http_server_thread`**: listens on **`0.0.0.0:WEB_HTTP_PORT`** (default **808**), separate from TCP **`TCP_PORT`** (8888).
- **Serves**
  - **`/`** — small dashboard: SVG arm (XY projection of FK polyline), limit dots (**green** = active, **muted red** = wired but open, **grey** = no switch), EE line, per‑joint **±0.5°** buttons, **EE −X / +X** (±0.35 units per click).
  - **`/api/state`** — JSON: joints, switches, EE, `polyline_xy`, `fk_ok`.
  - **`/api/jog_joint?j=&delta=`** / **`/api/jog_ee?dx=`** — enqueue motion.
- **`_web_cmd_queue`** drained on the **main loop** (same thread as motors) so **`set_target_angle`** runs safely.
- After axes are created, sets **`_http_axes_ref`** and starts the HTTP thread when **`ENABLE_WIFI`** and **`WIFI_SSID`** are set; serial log prints  
  `HTTP dashboard (same LAN): http://<pico-ip>:8080`.

## Usage
1. Set WiFi credentials and deploy from the GUI so **`ENABLE_WIFI`** is on and **`WEB_ARM_CONFIG`** is filled from your arm definition.
2. After boot, open **`http://<Pico-IP>:8080`** on the same LAN.
3. **`IK_USE_ELBOW_DOWN`** follows your **Elbow Down / Up** setting from the last deploy.

**Note:** EE Cartesian jogging needs **`ARM_LINK_LENGTHS`** (and matching joint count) injected — i.e. deploy with a normal arm config. **Non‑zero lateral offsets** disable analytical IK on the Pico (FK and joint jog still work).

  "contents": "# Fab Academy Week 11 — Networking, Communication & Connected Nodes\n\n**Course prompt (paraphrased):** *Design, build, and connect wired or wireless node(s) with network or bus addresses and a local input and/or output device(s).*\n\n**Project:** Robot Arm Simulator + Raspberry Pi Pico 2W embedded controller  \n**Repository:** Robot Arm Sim — desktop simulator (`Robot-Arm-Sim/`) and MicroPython firmware (`Robot-Arm-Sim/firmware/`)\n\nThis document maps each requirement of the assignment to concrete artifacts in this repository so it can be submitted as Week 11 documentation (HTML export, PDF, or GitLab Pages).\n\n---\n\n## 1. Assignment criteria → evidence\n\n| Requirement | How this project satisfies it |\n|---------------|-------------------------------|\n| **Design** | System architecture: PC runs IK, trajectory generation, and visualization; Pico executes motor stepping, optional homing, and networking. Geometry and motor parameters are configured in the GUI and injected into firmware at deploy time (`hardware/micropython_deployer.py`). |\n| **Build** | Fabricated stack: (1) desktop application on a host PC, (2) RP2040-based **Pico 2W** running **MicroPython**, (3) motor drivers (e.g. ULN2003 + 28BYJ-48, or STEP/DIR), (4) optional **limit / home switches** on GPIO inputs. |\n| **Connect wired or wireless** | **Wired:** USB serial (CDC) between PC and Pico — used for flashing, raw REPL deploy, and runtime control. **Wireless:** Pico joins a Wi‑Fi infrastructure (STA), exposes a **TCP** server for the same logical protocol as USB. |\n| **Network or bus addresses** | **USB:** serial port identifier (e.g. `COM7` on Windows, `/dev/ttyACM0` on Linux) selects the device. **Wi‑Fi:** **IPv4 address + TCP port** (default control channel **8888**; optional onboard **HTTP dashboard** on **8080**) uniquely identifies the node on the LAN. Messages are line-oriented text (`J0:…,J1:…`) — a simple application-layer protocol on top of the transport. |\n| **Local input and/or output** | **Outputs:** GPIO to motor drivers (step/direction or 28BYJ coil patterns), optional RC servo PWM, onboard **LED** toggle for link checks. **Inputs:** optional **home/limit** pins per joint (`home_pin` in motor configuration), read in the main loop for homing sequences and status. |\n\nTogether, these satisfy the spirit of Week 11: a **networked embedded node** with explicit **addressing**, **local actuation**, and **local sensing**, integrated with a host application.\n\n---\n\n## 2. System overview\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n    subgraph host[\"Host PC\"]\n        SIM[\"Simulator GUI\\nIK / animation\"]\n        USB[\"USB CDC serial\"]\n        WIFI_CLIENT[\"TCP client\\nsame protocol\"]\n    end\n    subgraph pico[\"Pico 2W node\"]\n        MP[\"MicroPython\\nmain.py firmware\"]\n        STA[\"Wi‑Fi STA\\nDHCP IP\"]\n        TCP[\"TCP :8888\\ncontrol + upload\"]\n        HTTP[\"HTTP :8080\\noptional dashboard\"]\n        GPIO_OUT[\"GPIO → motors\\nLED\"]\n        GPIO_IN[\"GPIO ← limits\"]\n    end\n    SIM --> USB\n    SIM --> WIFI_CLIENT\n    USB --> MP\n    WIFI_CLIENT --> STA --> TCP\n    TCP --> MP\n    MP --> GPIO_OUT\n    GPIO_IN --> MP\n```\n\n**Roles**\n\n- **Host node:** Planning, visualization, operator interface.\n- **Embedded node (Pico):** Real-time follower — converts streamed joint angles to steps or servo PWM, enforces configured limits, acceleration, and optional homing.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Addressing (explicit)\n\n| Layer | Wired (USB) | Wireless (Wi‑Fi) |\n|-------|-------------|-------------------|\n| Physical | USB cable to Pico | 2.4 GHz IEEE 802.11 (typical home lab AP) |\n| Device selection | Serial **COM port** or `/dev/ttyACM*` | **IP address** (shown after association, e.g. `192.168.1.42`) |\n| Service | CDC ACM serial stream | **TCP port** — default **8888** for control stream and firmware upload negotiation |\n| Extra | — | **HTTP** on **8080** for browser dashboard (FK/IK snapshot, joint jog, limit indicators) when enabled in firmware |\n\nThe Pico is therefore unambiguously reachable as **`IP:8888`** on the LAN for the simulator’s Hardware panel and **`http://IP:8080`** for the optional web UI.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Local outputs\n\n- **Motors:** Stepper channels (28BYJ half-step or STEP/DIR drivers) pull joints toward streamed angle targets with accel-limited stepping (`Robot-Arm-Sim/firmware/pico_control_script.py`).\n- **Servo (optional):** PWM output on a configured GPIO for RC servos.\n- **Indicator:** Board **LED** toggled via serial/Wi‑Fi command for connectivity checks.\n\nThese are **local** to the microcontroller — no cloud dependency.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Local inputs\n\n- **Home / limit switches:** Optional **digital GPIO** per joint (`home_pin`, polarity `NO`/`NC`). Firmware reads pins during homing and optional streaming so pressed vs released state is visible on the PC and on the HTTP dashboard (when Wi‑Fi is enabled).\n\nEven one switch demonstrates **local input**; multiple joints can each expose a limit channel.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Protocol (communication contract)\n\nHost → Pico messages are ASCII lines, for example:\n\n```text\nJ0:12.34,J1:-5.67,J2:10.00,J3:0.00\n```\n\nPico → Host acknowledges with `OK` or error lines — see `Robot-Arm-Sim/hardware/protocol.py` and firmware header comments. **Wi‑Fi upload** uses a separate line protocol (`UPLOAD_BEGIN`, chunked hex payloads) so firmware can be replaced over the air once the device already runs a compatible stack.\n\nThis is intentionally simple so it doubles as a **serial field bus** idiom (logical addressing by joint index `J0`…`Jn`).\n\n---\n\n## 7. Safety & ethics (documentation requirement)\n\n- Treat moving mechanisms as **pinch and collision hazards**; use **E-stop**, current limits, and clear workspace rules.\n- Wi‑Fi control assumes a **trusted LAN** — there is no cryptographic pairing in the educational firmware path; document that limitation for instructors.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Related documents\n\n- [**FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md**](FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md) — full project write-up.\n- [**ARCHITECTURE.md**](ARCHITECTURE.md) — simulator internals.\n- [**AI_HANDOFF.md**](AI_HANDOFF.md) — subsystem map for developers.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Submission checklist (student-facing)\n\n- [ ] Replace placeholders with **your name**, **Fab Lab / region**, and **license** if required by your instructor.\n- [ ] Add **photos**: Pico + wiring, motor drivers, limit switches (if used), screenshot of Hardware panel with IP/port.\n- [ ] Add **short video** (optional): jog from simulator over USB, then repeat over Wi‑Fi.\n- [ ] Link this file from your **Fab Academy documentation repository** or GitLab Pages index.\n\n---\n\n*This file is intended to satisfy the Fab Academy **Week 11** prompt on connected nodes, addressing, and local I/O when paired with the implemented codebase and hardware described above.*\n"

# Networking and Communication

This week, I am adding wireless capabilities to the robot arm's control software that was generated using claude. The majority of the code this week is AI generated, as I have no idea how to code and rely heavily on AI for a majority of my coding projects. But, I am good at figuring things out. For a better look at how the software works, please visit [the repo](https://github.com/Max-Negrin/Robot-Arm-Sim). For a brief summary, the software takes a coordinate input (or set of coordinates) and calculates the joint angles, given joint lengths, numbers, and an optional end effector constraint (to set it to X degrees as long as there is a third link). It then streams them via serial to a Pico 2W, a cheap and readily available MCU in out lab. The Pico also must handle parts of the homing sequence, in sensing when the limit switch makes contact and streaming that to the computer. To complete the assignment for the week, I will add wireless capabilites to allow the computer to stream joint positions to the Pico, and for the Pico to send limit switch positions back to the computer, without a physical connection. You can find a thorough summary of the control software [here](../../Final%20Project/Software.md).

  "contents": "---\ntitle: Networking and Communications\ndescription: Fab Academy Week — how LAN TCP connects the simulator to the Pico 2W (implementation detail).\n---\n\n# Networking and Communication\n\nThis page explains **how** the desktop simulator talks to the **Raspberry Pi Pico 2W** over the lab network: which **libraries**, which **methods**, and where the **scripts** live. The setup described here assumes you operate **over Wi‑Fi** (TCP/IP on the LAN)—that is how the assignment requirements are met in practice.\n\nMost of the implementation was built with AI assistance (Claude / Cursor). I focus on **what each layer does** so I can debug it when something breaks.\n\nRepository: **[github.com/Max-Negrin/Robot-Arm-Sim](https://github.com/Max-Negrin/Robot-Arm-Sim)**\n\nFor the formal assignment checklist (nodes, addressing, local I/O), see **[FAB_WEEK11_ASSIGNMENT.md](FAB_WEEK11_ASSIGNMENT.md)**. For full software architecture, see **[FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md](FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md)**.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Big picture\n\n| Layer | Role |\n|-------|------|\n| **PC — Python / PyQt6** | IK, animation, Hardware panel. Streams joint angles as **text lines** to the Pico. |\n| **Transport** | **TCP socket** to **`IP:8888`** on the LAN (default port). Same **application protocol** no matter how you reached the Pico during development. |\n| **Pico — MicroPython `main.py`** | Joins the access point, listens on **TCP**, parses lines, drives GPIO to motors, reads limit pins. |\n\n**Addressing:** The Pico is identified by **`IPv4 + TCP port`** (for example `192.168.1.42:8888`). That satisfies “network addresses” for Week 11 documentation.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Host side — Python libraries and modules\n\n| Library / module | What it is used for |\n|------------------|---------------------|\n| **`socket` (stdlib)** | Client TCP connection: `socket.create_connection((host, port), …)` |\n| **`threading`** | Background **TX** and **RX** loops so the GUI never blocks on the network |\n| **`queue.Queue`** | Non-blocking queue of outbound bytes; producer = GUI, consumer = TX thread |\n| **`hardware.protocol`** | **`encode_angles()`**, **`angles_changed()`**, **`encode_sync_line()`** — shared encoding with the serial driver |\n| **`hardware.pico_wifi_interface.PicoWifiInterface`** | Drop-in transport class with the **same public methods** as the USB `PicoInterface` (`connect`, `send_joint_angles`, `send_raw`, `disconnect`) |\n\nThe GUI does **not** talk to sockets directly. It holds a **`_hardware`** reference that implements **`send_joint_angles(radians)`** and **`send_raw(text)`** — whether traffic goes over USB serial or TCP is decided by which interface class was constructed when you clicked **Connect**.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Message encoding (`hardware/protocol.py`)\n\nAngles inside the app are **radians**. On the wire they must be **degrees**, ASCII, comma-separated, newline-terminated:\n\n```python\n# hardware/protocol.py — core encoding (abbreviated)\ndef encode_angles(angles_rad: list[float]) -> bytes:\n    parts = [f\"J{i}:{math.degrees(a):.4f}\" for i, a in enumerate(angles_rad)]\n    return (\",\".join(parts) + \"\\n\").encode(\"utf-8\")\n```\n\nAfter reconnecting, the PC sends a **`SYNC:`** line so the Pico adopts the simulator pose **without** sprinting from zero:\n\n```python\ndef encode_sync_line(angles_rad: list[float]) -> str:\n    body = \",\".join(f\"J{i}:{math.degrees(a):.4f}\" for i, a in enumerate(angles_rad))\n    return f\"SYNC:{body}\\n\"\n```\n\nTiny angle changes are suppressed so the link is not flooded (`angles_changed`, threshold **`UPDATE_THRESHOLD_RAD`**).\n\n---\n\n## 4. TCP client — `PicoWifiInterface` (`hardware/pico_wifi_interface.py`)\n\n### 4.1 Connect\n\n`connect(host, port=8888)` uses **`socket.create_connection`** with retries (the Pico may still be joining the LAN). It waits until it sees the firmware **ready banner**, then sends a probe **`J0:0.00\\n`** and checks for **`OK`** — proving the line-oriented parser on the Pico is alive.\n\n### 4.2 Threads and queue\n\nAfter a successful connect:\n\n1. **`threading.Thread`** **`_tx_loop`** — drains **`queue.Queue`** and calls **`sock.sendall(msg)`** for each queued payload.\n2. **`threading.Thread`** **`_rx_loop`** — **`sock.recv`**, splits on **`\\n`**, passes each line to **`rx_callback`** (the GUI logs Pico text like **`OK`** or **`PINS:`**).\n\n### 4.3 Sending angles from the GUI\n\n```python\ndef send_joint_angles(self, angles_rad: list[float]) -> None:\n    if not self._connected:\n        return\n    if not angles_changed(self._last_angles, angles_rad):\n        return\n    msg = encode_angles(angles_rad)\n    # … enqueue msg on self._tx_queue (drops oldest if queue full)\n```\n\nSo the **hot path** is: **`encode_angles`** → **bytes** → **TX queue** → **TCP socket**.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Feedback — limit switches back to the PC\n\nHoming uses GPIO pins configured per joint (`home_pin` in the motor JSON). When you want **live** switch visibility on the host, the simulator sends text commands over the **same TCP session**:\n\n- **`PIN_STREAM_ON`** / **`PIN_STREAM_OFF`** — firmware toggles periodic **`PINS:`** lines with live GPIO reads.\n\nThose responses arrive on the **RX thread** and surface through the same **`rx_callback`** path as **`OK`**.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Pico side — MicroPython (overview)\n\nThe deployed **`main.py`** (template: `Robot-Arm-Sim/firmware/pico_control_script.py`) runs the motor loop and network I/O. Conceptually on boot it:\n\n1. Brings up **`network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)`**, connects with stored **SSID / password**, obtains an address via DHCP.\n2. Opens **`socket.socket()`**, **`bind((\"\", TCP_PORT))`**, **`listen(1)`** — default **`TCP_PORT`** is **8888**.\n3. Uses **`_thread.start_new_thread`** so incoming TCP lines are pushed into a queue the **main loop** drains — **same `_handle_line()` parser** used for angle streaming and **`PIN_STREAM`** handling.\n\nIllustrative excerpt (structure only):\n\n```python\nimport network\nimport socket\nimport _thread\n\nwlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)\nwlan.active(True)\nwlan.connect(WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD)\n# … wait until wlan.isconnected()\n\nsrv = socket.socket()\nsrv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)\nsrv.bind((\"\", TCP_PORT))\nsrv.listen(1)\n\ndef network_reader():\n    conn = None\n    while True:\n        # accept client, recv bytes, split on \\n, append lines to rx queue …\n        ...\n\n_thread.start_new_thread(network_reader, ())\n```\n\nThe **parser** turns **`J0:12.34,J1:…`** into target angles and calls **`set_target_angle`** on each axis object — identical logic whether bytes arrived from USB or from Wi‑Fi.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Optional browser dashboard (same LAN)\n\nThe firmware can also serve a small **HTTP** page on **`WEB_HTTP_PORT`** (default **8080**) with joint/limit readouts and jog buttons. That uses another **`socket`** listener in a background thread and JSON **`/api/state`** — handy for demos without the Python app. Details are embedded in the firmware source and summarized in **[FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md](FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md)**.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Integrity note\n\nAI wrote most of the code; my job in documentation is to show **which standard pieces** connect (**TCP**, **`socket`**, **`threading`**, **`encode_angles`**, MicroPython **`network` + socket server**). That is what instructors usually want for “explain your networking week.”\n\n---\n\n*See also: **[FAB_WEEK11_ASSIGNMENT.md](FAB_WEEK11_ASSIGNMENT.md)** for criteria mapping and diagrams.*\n"

Application details (IK, angle formatting) are summarized briefly at the end.\n\nRepository: **[github.com/Max-Negrin/Robot-Arm-Sim](https://github.com/Max-Negrin/Robot-Arm-Sim)**\n\nRelated: **[FAB_WEEK11_ASSIGNMENT.md](FAB_WEEK11_ASSIGNMENT.md)** · **[FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md](FAB_PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md)**\n\n---\n\n## 1. Protocol choice: TCP on port 8888\n\nThe link between simulator and Pico is **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol), not UDP.\n\n| Aspect | Why it matters here |\n|--------|---------------------|\n| **Reliable, ordered delivery** | Joint commands and acknowledgements must not be dropped or reordered arbitrarily. |\n| **Single bidirectional session** | One **connected socket** carries **host → Pico** commands and **Pico → host** lines (`OK`, `ERR:`, `PINS:`, banners) on the **same** TCP connection (**full-duplex**). |\n| **Stream abstraction** | TCP delivers a **byte stream**; both sides buffer and split on **newline (`\\n`)** to recover **lines** (text protocol). |\n\nDefault **TCP port** for robot control: **`8888`** (`DEFAULT_PORT` in `hardware/pico_wifi_interface.py`). The Pico **listens** (`bind` + `listen`); the PC **connects** as **client** (`socket.create_connection`).\n\n---\n\n## 2. Where Wi‑Fi fits in the stack\n\nRough layering (top = closest to your code):\n\n```text\n Application  │  Line-oriented text (J0:…, SYNC:, PIN_STREAM_ON, …)\n ─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n Transport    │  TCP — port 8888 (control), optionally port 8080 (HTTP dashboard)\n ─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n Network      │  IPv4 — addressing on the LAN (often DHCP-assigned)\n ─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n Link / PHY   │  IEEE 802.11 (Wi‑Fi) — Pico in STA (station) mode joins an access point\n```\n\n**Wi‑Fi** provides radio + association with an **SSID**; once associated, the Pico gets an **IPv4 address** (typically via **DHCP** from the access point). Your laptop uses **the same LAN**. Traffic between PC and Pico is **IP routing / switching**, not “USB serial tunneling.”\n\n---\n\n## 3. Addressing and discovery\n\n| Concept | In this project |\n|---------|-----------------|\n| **Host identification** | **IPv4 address** of the Pico on the LAN, e.g. **`192.168.1.42`**. |\n| **Service identification** | **`IP : TCP port`** → e.g. **`192.168.1.42:8888`** for control. |\n| **How the IP is known** | Typed into the Hardware panel after reading it from the Pico **boot log** (the firmware prints something like “WiFi connected: x.x.x.x”) or from your router/DHCP client list. |\n\nThere is no multicast DNS requirement in the stock stack: **you supply the IP** the same way you’d SSH to a Raspberry Pi.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Roles: TCP client vs TCP server\n\n| Side | Role | Berkeley sockets pattern |\n|------|------|---------------------------|\n| **PC (Python)** | **TCP client** | `socket.create_connection((host, port))` → **connected socket** to Pico |\n| **Pico (MicroPython)** | **TCP server** | `socket()` → `setsockopt(SO_REUSEADDR)` → `bind((\"\", port))` → `listen(1)` → `accept()` per client |\n\nOnly **one** client connection is typical (`listen(1)` backlog semantics); the simulator holds that connection open for streaming.\n\n**`SO_REUSEADDR`** on the Pico allows quick rebinding after restarts during development—standard when iterating on firmware.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Connection lifecycle (what actually happens)\n\n**PC — `PicoWifiInterface.connect()`** (`hardware/pico_wifi_interface.py`):\n\n1. **TCP connect** — **`socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=3)`** in a **retry loop** until **`CONNECT_TIMEOUT` (30 s)** elapses. Failures while the Pico is still booting or joining Wi‑Fi surface as **`ConnectionRefusedError`** / **`OSError`** → brief sleep and retry.\n2. **Application handshake** — wait until incoming bytes contain **`firmware ready`** / **`Robot Arm Pico Controller ready`** (banner drain).\n3. **Probe** — send **`J0:0.00\\n`** and confirm **`OK`** appears in the receive buffer (proves the line parser is running, not some other service on that port).\n\nThen the code starts **two threads**:\n\n- **TX thread** — **`sock.sendall(bytes)`** from a **`queue.Queue`** (GUI enqueues; never blocks the Qt event loop).\n- **RX thread** — **`sock.recv(256)`** in a loop, buffer until **`\\\\n`**, dispatch each line to **`rx_callback`**.\n\n**Pico —** after **WLAN STA** is up and **`wlan.isconnected()`**:\n\n1. **`srv.bind((\"\", TCP_PORT))`** — listen on **all interfaces** (`\"\"`) on port **8888**.\n2. **`accept()`** loop → one **client socket** for the PC.\n3. Received bytes are framed into lines and fed into the **same command parser** as the rest of the firmware.\n\nSo the **networking** story is: **association → IPv4 → TCP listen → TCP connect → persistent session → newline-framed messages.**\n\n---\n\n## 6. Multiple TCP services on one device\n\nThe Pico can expose **more than one TCP listener** on **different ports**:\n\n| Port | Purpose |\n|------|---------|\n| **8888** | Primary **control** channel — angle lines, `STOP`, `PIN_STREAM_*`, firmware upload protocol (`UPLOAD_*`), etc. |\n| **8080** | Optional **HTTP** server — browser dashboard (`WEB_HTTP_PORT` in firmware). Separate **`socket.bind`** / accept loop from the control server. |\n\nBoth ride on the **same Wi‑Fi IP**. Only the **port number** selects which handler receives the connection.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Throughput and timing (LAN vs serial mental model)\n\nOn **TCP over Wi‑Fi**, the code treats the link as **high enough bandwidth** for lines of ASCII that joint streams need. The GUI still uses a nominal **`_baud = 921600`** on **`PicoWifiInterface`** **only** as a **hint** for rate-limiting how often **`J0:…`** lines are sent—it is **not** UART speed.\n\nLatency is dominated by **Wi‑Fi**, OS scheduling, and Python threads—but for a lab LAN it is usually **milliseconds**, fine for human-scale robot streaming.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Failure modes (debugging the network)\n\n| Symptom | Typical cause |\n|---------|----------------|\n| **Connection refused** | Nothing listening on **8888** yet (Pico still booting), wrong IP, or wrong port. |\n| **Timeout / no banner** | Pico associated but firmware not ready; firewall blocking TCP (rare on same LAN); wrong IP. |\n| **Connects but probe fails** | Another process grabbed the port, or firmware hung. |\n| **Dropped mid-session** | Sleep/power, AP kicked client, cable-equivalent resets — RX thread reports disconnect. |\n\nChecks that usually work: **same SSID/LAN as laptop**, **ping IP**, **correct port**, **watch Pico serial boot log for IP**.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Application payload (short — not “networking,” but it rides on TCP)\n\nAngles are encoded as ASCII lines (radians → degrees in **`hardware/protocol.py`**):\n\n```python\nparts = [f\"J{i}:{math.degrees(a):.4f}\" for i, a in enumerate(angles_rad)]\nmsg = (\",\".join(parts) + \"\\n\").encode(\"utf-8\")   # → TCP via sendall\n```\n\nResponses (`OK`, `PINS:…`) return on the **same TCP socket** — **`PIN_STREAM_ON`** enables periodic limit-read lines over that session.\n\n---\n\n## 10. Integrity note\n\nAI-assisted implementation is documented honestly; the **networking** takeaway for assessment is naming concrete mechanisms: **Wi‑Fi STA**, **IPv4/DHCP**, **TCP client/server**, **ports 8888 (and optionally 8080)**, **persistent connection**, **threaded I/O**, **newline framing**.\n\n---\n\n*Criteria checklist and diagram: **[FAB_WEEK11_ASSIGNMENT.md](FAB_WEEK11_ASSIGNMENT.md)**.*\n",

### What’s new / sharper

- **Opening** ties Week 11 requirements (addresses + I/O) to **STA/DHCP + TCP**, then spells out **your execution loop**: mirror serial/TCP APIs → flash STA+firmware → **Deploy / DHCP IP / Connect / banner→probe→OK**.
- **Layer table**: PHY (**802.11 STA**), **IPv4/DHCP**, **TCP (`AF_INET`, stream)**, **application framing** (delimiter `\n`, not length-prefix).
- **Addressing**: `bind("")`, **`listen(1)`**, **`accept`**, **`SO_REUSEADDR`**, manual discovery vs mDNS.
- **TCP rationale**: reliability, single session, full duplex; explicit **`recv` coalescing** / **no message boundaries**.
- **Host internals**: **`CONNECT_TIMEOUT` vs per-connect timeout**, banner sync, **`J0:0.00\n`** probe, **`Lock`** around **`sock`**, **bounded queue (32)** drop-oldest policy, TX/RX thread behavior, **`UPDATE_THRESHOLD_RAD`** back-pressure on chatter.
- **Pico internals**: **`WLAN(STA_IF)`**, lwIP-ish DHCP wording, secondary **`_thread`** + **`_wifi_rx`** drain into **`_handle_line`** (single parser).
- **HTTP**: second TCP listener / shared IPv4 (technical aside).
- **Failure modes**: map symptoms to **TCP vs application vs PHY**, **`ECONNREFUSED`**, **`recv` returns b''**, ping vs **LISTEN** distinction.

  "new_string": "Limit visibility: `PIN_STREAM_ON` toggles periodic `PINS:` telemetry—still the same TCP socket; the RX thread delivers lines identically.\n\n---\n\n## Joint streaming end-to-end (simulator → Pico)\n\n### Host: where angles come from\n\nThe main window runs a fast Qt timer (`gui.py`). Each tick calls `_try_send_hardware_update()`, which is the integration point for hardware.\n\nIf hardware sync is enabled (`hardware_panel.is_hardware_sync_enabled()`), the GUI builds a vector of joint angles in radians from the current arm state: `_gravity_adjusted_hardware_angles_rad()`, then applies `_apply_direction_backlash_to_angles()` so commanded angles match the backlash model before leaving the PC.\n\nStreaming is intentionally rate-limited: `_hardware_angle_stream_min_interval_s()` estimates how often a single `J0,…,Jn` line can be sent without overrunning the logical link capacity. It assumes ~10 bits per byte for timing purposes, uses the interface’s `_baud` hint (`921600` on `PicoWifiInterface`—not physical UART speed, just a budget for line frequency), estimates bytes per line from joint count, caps effective line rate (higher caps while `animator.is_running`). Until that interval elapses, `send_joint_angles` is not called again.\n\nDuring homing (`_homing_active`), angle streaming is suppressed so `HOME` sequences are not fighting constant `J0:…` updates.\n\n### Host: encoding and transmit path\n\n`MainWindow._hardware` holds either `PicoInterface` or `PicoWifiInterface`; both implement `send_joint_angles(angles_rad: list[float])`.\n\nIn `PicoWifiInterface.send_joint_angles` (`hardware/pico_wifi_interface.py`):\n\n1. If no TCP session, return.\n2. Compare against `_last_angles` using `angles_changed()` from `hardware/protocol.py` against `UPDATE_THRESHOLD_RAD` (~1e-5 rad). Identical poses do not enqueue traffic.\n3. `encode_angles()` builds UTF-8 bytes: comma-separated `Ji:deg` with four fractional digits plus `\\n`.\n4. Enqueue on `queue.Queue(maxsize=32)`. If full, drop the oldest item then enqueue—bounded backlog under animation bursts.\n\nA daemon TX thread blocks on the queue and calls `sock.sendall(msg)` so the Qt thread never blocks on the network.\n\n### Connect alignment\n\nOn connect, `seed_pose_to_match_host()` sends `STOP\\n` then `encode_sync_line(...)` (`SYNC:J0:…`). Firmware interprets `SYNC:` as “set logical pose without a catch-up sprint”—important after TCP reconnect when motor state and sim state must match.\n\n### Device: ingress and actuation\n\nOn the Pico, bytes from the TCP client arrive on the network thread; complete lines are queued for the main loop (same pattern as USB stdin). The main loop calls `_handle_line(line, reply_fn)`.\n\nIf the line matches `J0:…,J1:…` without a leading keyword, `parse_command()` splits into `{joint_index: degrees}` and for each loaded axis calls `axis.set_target_angle(degrees)`. Stepper firmware converts targets to step counts and follows with accel-limited stepping toward those targets in the periodic motor update.\n\n---\n\n## HTTP dashboard (embedded server on Pico)\n\nThe dashboard is a second TCP server on the microcontroller, independent of port 8888 control traffic.\n\n### Socket setup\n\n`_web_http_server_thread()` in `firmware/pico_control_script.py`:\n\n- `socket.socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)`\n- `setsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, 1)`\n- `bind((\"0.0.0.0\", WEB_HTTP_PORT))` — default 8080 after deploy injection (`WEB_HTTP_PORT` in `WEB_ARM_CONFIG` block)\n- `listen(2)`, `settimeout(1.0)` on the listening socket so `accept()` can be interrupted periodically without blocking forever\n\nThe thread loop `accept()`s connections, reads until `\\r\\n\\r\\n` (minimal HTTP request framing), parses the first line for `METHOD path[?query] HTTP/x`.\n\n### Routes (hand-built HTTP/1.0)\n\nNo Flask or MicroDot dependency—responses are concatenated strings:\n\n- `GET /` or `/index.html` — serves one large HTML document with inline CSS and `<script>`: `fetch('/api/state')` on an interval, SVG polyline for arm XY projection, buttons that `fetch('/api/jog_joint?j=&delta=')` and `/api/jog_ee?dx=`.\n- `GET /api/state` — builds a Python dict (joint angles, switch states, FK-derived EE, `polyline_xy`), `json.dumps`, `Content-Type: application/json`.\n- `GET /api/jog_joint?…` / `/api/jog_ee?…` — parses query string, appends tuples to `_web_cmd_queue`; returns short `{\"ok\":true}` JSON.\n\nReply path: `HTTP/1.0 200 OK`, `Content-Type`, `Connection: close`, `Content-Length`, blank line, body bytes—all sent with `conn.send`.\n\n### Shared state with motion\n\n`_http_axes_ref` points at the live `axes` list after motors are constructed; the HTTP thread reads angles and GPIO for JSON snapshots only.\n\nJog requests must not call motor APIs from the HTTP thread: `_web_cmd_queue` is drained on the main motor loop via `_apply_web_command()`, which calls `set_target_angle` or IK-assisted EE nudge—same safety as TCP-delivered commands.\n\n`main()` starts `_web_http_server_thread` with `_thread.start_new_thread` once axes exist and the STA link is in use, so HTTP and motor timing stay loosely coupled.\n\n---\n\n## Failure modes (technical)",
